primary_source_citation.title: FAA Pilot's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 5) Technical Reference: Four Forces of Flight & Three-Axis Primary Flight Controls

1.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: In steady unaccelerated level flight, upward Lift equals downward Weight and forward Thrust equals rearward Drag.
core_mechanism_bullets: 1. Lift vs. Weight (Vertical Axis): Curved upper camber accelerates airflow (Bernoulli lower pressure) while downward trailing wash (Newton 3rd Law) generates upward Lift.
2. Thrust vs. Drag (Longitudinal Axis): Propeller or turbofan accelerates air rearward to overcome parasite form drag and lift-induced wingtip vortex drag.
3. Roll (Ailerons) & Pitch (Elevator): Moving yoke left/right moves outboard wing ailerons oppositely to Roll; pulling yoke aft raises tail Elevator to Pitch nose up.
4. Yaw (Rudder Pedals) & Coordinated Turn: Foot pedals deflect vertical tail Rudder left/right around the vertical axis to counter adverse yaw and keep the inclinometer ball centered.
1.worked_field_example: Exceeding the wing's critical angle of attack near 16 to 18 degrees separates smooth airflow over the upper camber and triggers a stall.
1.counselor_tabletop_demo: Use a model airplane to demonstrate how opposite aileron deflection rolls the wings while elevator and rudder control pitch and yaw.
1.real_world_connection_box: FAA Pilot's Handbook Aerodynamics Standard: In steady unaccelerated level flight, upward Lift equals downward Weight and forward Thrust equals rearward Drag. Ailerons control Roll around the longitudinal axis, the elevator controls Pitch around the lateral axis, and the rudder controls Yaw.
1.grounded_citation_label: Verified: Scouting America Pamphlet + FAA Pilot's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 5)

primary_source_citation.title: FAA Pilot's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 8) Technical Reference: The Cockpit 'Six-Pack': Pitot-Static vs. Gyroscopic Instruments

2.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Three Pitot-Static instruments measure air pressure to display Airspeed, Altitude, and Vertical Speed.
core_mechanism_bullets: Pitot + Static: Airspeed Indicator (Knots): Subtracts static port pressure from forward ram-air Pitot pressure; color arcs mark white flap range, green normal, yellow caution, red Vne.
Static Pressure: Altimeter & VSI: Aneroid wafers expand as ambient pressure drops with altitude (~1 inHg per 1,000 ft), driving the 3-pointer Altimeter and ft/min VSI.
Gyroscopic: Attitude & Heading Indicators: Artificial horizon shows real-time bank angle and pitch relative to horizon; Heading Indicator tracks magnetic compass heading.
Engine & Tachometer Monitoring: RPM tachometer, oil temperature, and oil pressure gauges give immediate early warning of powerplant anomalies.
2.worked_field_example: If the wing pitot tube blocks while the static port stays open, the Airspeed Indicator fails while the Altimeter and VSI continue operating.
2.counselor_tabletop_demo: Trace the red ram-air pitot line and blue static line to the three pressure gauges, then identify the three gyroscopic gauges.
2.real_world_connection_box: FAA Flight Instruments (FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 8) Standard: Three Pitot-Static instruments measure air pressure to display Airspeed, Altitude, and Vertical Speed. Three Gyroscopic instruments use spinning rotor rigidity to display Attitude, Magnetic Heading, and Rate of Turn.
2.grounded_citation_label: Verified: Scouting America Pamphlet + FAA Pilot's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-25C Ch. 8)
2.bespoke_visual_caption: Cockpit six-pack cutaway linking the Airspeed Indicator, Altimeter, and VSI to pitot-static pressure and the remaining three gauges to gyroscopes.
v47_primary_source_bullets: Three Pitot-Static instruments measure air pressure to display Airspeed, Altitude, and Vertical Speed.
Three Gyroscopic instruments use spinning rotor rigidity to display Attitude, Magnetic Heading, and Rate of Turn.

primary_source_citation.title: FAA Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C) Technical Reference: Cessna 172 Walk-Around Preflight & Runway Magnetic Numbering

3.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Runway numbers drop the last digit of magnetic compass heading so aircraft can take off and land directly into the wind.
core_mechanism_bullets: Cockpit Safety & A-R-R-O-W Check: Verify Magnetos OFF, Master switch OFF, control lock removed, and Airworthiness, Registration, Radio, Operating Handbook, Weight & Balance.
Fuel Sump Drain & Quantity Check: Visually dip both wing tanks and drain low-point fuel sumps into a clear tester cup to verify zero water globules or debris.
Airframe, Hinges, Pitot & Prop Walk-Around: Remove red 'Remove Before Flight' Pitot cover, inspect propeller leading edge for nicks, check tire inflation, and test all control hinges.
Runway Markings, Windsock & Phonetic ATC: Read windsock direction to pick the headwind runway, hold short of double solid/dashed yellow lines, and use ICAO Alpha-Bravo-Charlie radio calls.
3.worked_field_example: When the airport windsock indicates wind blowing from 270 degrees magnetic (due West), pilots depart and land on Runway 27.
3.counselor_tabletop_demo: Inspect a clear fuel-tester cup sample to see how heavier water settles below aviation fuel at the bottom of the cylinder.
3.real_world_connection_box: FAA Airplane Flying Handbook Preflight Standard: Runway numbers drop the last digit of magnetic compass heading so aircraft can take off and land directly into the wind. A walk-around preflight inspection verifies water-free fuel sump samples, control hinges, landing gear tires, and pitot covers.
3.grounded_citation_label: Verified: Scouting America Pamphlet + FAA Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C)
3.bespoke_visual_caption: Airfield ramp walk-around showing a flight instructor and Scouts inspecting a fuel tester, landing gear, and red pitot cover near a windsock.
3.v47_slide_title: FAA Airplane Flying Handbook Preflight Standard

primary_source_citation.title: FAA STEM AVSED & EAA Young Eagles Technical Reference: Aviation & Aerospace Career Pathways, FAA Certificates & STEM Roles

4.rule_of_thumb_mnemonic: Student pilots can solo a glider at age 14 and a powered aircraft at age 16 before earning a Private Pilot Certificate at age 17.
core_mechanism_bullets: 1. FAA Pilot Certificate Ladder: Student Pilot solo at 16 (glider at 14) -> Private Pilot (PPL) at 17 -> Instrument Rating (IFR) -> Commercial (CPL) -> Airline Transport (ATP).
2. Airframe & Powerplant (A&P) Mechanic: FAA-certificated aviation maintenance technicians inspect turbines, avionics, hydraulics, and structural composites before every flight.
3. FAA Air Traffic Controller (ATC): Tower, TRACON approach, and En Route center controllers sequence thousands of daily flights safely through radar and ADS-B separation.
4. Aerospace & Unmanned Systems Engineer: Designs wings, propulsion, fly-by-wire avionics, autonomous Part 107 drones, and spacecraft in wind tunnels and CFD simulators.
4.worked_field_example: Through the EAA Young Eagles program, Scouts ages 8 to 17 can log an introductory flight with a certificated pilot at zero cost.
4.counselor_tabletop_demo: Compare the training pathways and daily responsibilities of a cockpit pilot, tower controller, FAA A&P technician, and wind-tunnel engineer.
4.real_world_connection_box: FAA Airman Certification & STEM AVSED Standard: Student pilots can solo a glider at age 14 and a powered aircraft at age 16 before earning a Private Pilot Certificate at age 17. Safe flight operations depend equally on FAA Airframe and Powerplant mechanics, Air Traffic Controllers, and aerospace engineers.
4.grounded_citation_label: Verified: Scouting America Pamphlet + FAA STEM AVSED & 14 CFR Part 61
4.bespoke_visual_caption: Four-panel aviation career vignette depicting an airline pilot, tower air traffic controller, turbofan A&P mechanic, and wind-tunnel engineer.
4.v47_slide_title: FAA Airman Certification & STEM AVSED Standard
v47_primary_source_bullets: Student pilots can solo a glider at age 14 and a powered aircraft at age 16 before earning a Private Pilot Certificate at age 17.
Safe flight operations depend equally on FAA Airframe and Powerplant mechanics, Air Traffic Controllers, and aerospace engineers.
